name: Beth Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What fills a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play keyboard for a wedding band, teach in my front-room studio and make short music cues, the pieces that play under local adverts. I have a music bachelor's and years of Saturday sets behind me, though I still practise a new singer's key before a job.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the household look like around that schedule?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Amir drives buses, and our two children are at school. We have a mortgage and about nine months of expenses saved; my music income is good and there are several bands and teaching rooms nearby. I use AI every day for invoices and rough chord charts, but my ear and the signed booking decide what goes out.

say: I'd welcome **quicker paperwork** while keeping the band responsible for the live set.
I'd tell couples the **chorus cue** still comes from players listening together.
think: Our **nine-month reserve** and booked teaching can cover a late advert fee.
I use **AI daily** for invoices and drafts but compare them with signed bookings.
do: Confirm **signed winter dates** and renew eight paid pupils this week.
Save **a hundred** from cleared advert fees after transport and children's shoes are paid.
feel: I feel **calm** because regular work and savings cover a delayed payment.
S0.quote: A neat invoice with the wrong fee is still the wrong fee.
fieldNote: Her **higher pay** and nine months saved let the family absorb a late advert cheque.
She uses **AI daily** for paperwork but checks the fee against the signed booking.

steps.text: Confirm signed band dates and renew eight paid pupils

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the wedding players that quicker paperwork is welcome. A couple still wants us to know when to bring the chorus in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the clever tools stay small, my booked Saturdays and pupils should keep paying. Nine months saved and Amir's bus wage can absorb a late advert cheque, though we still have a mortgage to meet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll confirm the band's signed winter dates and renew eight paid pupils for next term. After the next advert fee clears, I'll move a hundred into our mortgage reserve once transport and the children's shoes are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about this picture. A late cheque is annoying, but it would not empty the cupboard or cancel a lesson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has a late advert fee affected the household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An advert client paid a month late last spring. Amir covered the food bill, and I replaced the reserve money when the fee came through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you check the tool's invoices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use the invoice tool each day, but I compare its total with the signed booking before sending it. A neat invoice with the wrong fee is still the wrong fee.

say: I'd ask for **paid arranging hours** before signing away unlimited revisions.
I'd bring **fee evidence** to the musicians association.
think: About **one-third of my income** from cues and arranging may shrink soon.
Nine months saved cannot replace **ongoing lost fees** for the mortgage.
do: Compare **ten cue invoices** with new offers and take them to the association this month.
Learn a new **AI accompaniment tool** on owned tracks with paid-use licence and manual chord checks.
Require **written permission** for other voices; stop if chords are invented or melody is lost.
feel: I feel **anxious** about paid correction work disappearing despite household savings.
S1.quote: A full diary is not the same as a paid diary.
fieldNote: She expects **cue income** to fall, so higher pay and savings cannot by themselves keep the mortgage budget whole.
Her **new AI trial** includes ownership, paid-use licence, ear checks and written permission for other voices.

steps.text: Bring ten cue invoices and new client offers to musicians association
Test licensed accompaniment tool on own tracks and check every chord
Require written voice permission; stop for false chords or buried melody

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the bandleader to show us which paid arranging and advert-cue hours software will replace. I would bring the old fee sheet to the musicians association before agreeing to unlimited revisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nearly a third of my pay comes from short cues and arranging, and clients may buy fewer hours soon. Nine months saved is a good cushion, but a third less money would still change the mortgage budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll compare ten cue invoices with new client offers and bring them to the association. In the first year of change, I'll learn a new AI accompaniment tool on my own practice tracks only if its licence allows paid use, checking every chord by ear before a pupil hears it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about clients treating a machine draft as a reason to pay nothing for corrections. I can ask other bands for work. A full diary is not the same as a paid diary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Whose track could you safely test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will not upload a child's lesson or another singer's voice without written permission. If the tool invents a chord or buries a melody, I will stop and use my own recording.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the association ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want the association to ask for a minimum arranging fee and a revision limit in writing. I'll bring the invoices, not guess at a fair number in the meeting.

say: I'd ask venues for **written live fees** before AGI changes cue work.
I'd tell the band **robot players** follow thinking AGI by about three years.
think: **AGI in 2028** could remove cue fees before robots play around 2031.
Our **nine-month reserve** buys a search period, not permanent replacement income.
do: List **three income streams** and request written band dates now.
Apply **after 2028** if cue fees halve, only for a posted qualifying college role with pickup and written replacement net pay.
Keep **current pupils and dates** until a signed offer; ask lender about full interest before arrears if teaching falls.
feel: I feel **anxious** about rapid fee loss, with savings and local vacancies giving some control.
S2.quote: A vacancy from last year will not pay next month's mortgage.
fieldNote: Her **2028 thinking-work loss** precedes robot keyboard playing around 2031.
Her **college application** needs an actual opening, qualifying degree, child pickup and written net pay after travel.

steps.text: Keep pupils and band dates until signed offer; list income and request written live calls
Apply after 2028 if cue fees halve and posted college role accepts degree
Require pickup and written net pay after travel before leaving pupils or band
Ask lender before arrears if teaching falls; check total added interest before signing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the band that AGI by 2028 could write cues before robots can play keyboards around 2031. I would ask every venue to confirm live pay in writing now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cue and arranging work could go cheaply to AGI almost at once. Live weddings should last longer, but losing a third of my fees would strain the household even with Amir's wage and nine months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll list band, teaching and advert pay and ask for next year's band dates in writing. In the first year after 2028, if cue fees halve, I'll apply for a posted rehearsal-accompanist role at a local college only if my bachelor's qualifies, the hours fit child pickup and its written net pay after travel replaces the loss. I'll keep my current pupils and band dates until another contract is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the pace, but I have other schools and bands to approach. A vacancy from last year will not pay next month's mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the college role actually open?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The college filled an accompanist job in September. I'll ask to hear about the next posted opening, but I won't count it as income before an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the studio loses a teaching day too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If teaching also loses a day, Amir and I would ask the lender about temporary terms before arrears. We would check total added interest before signing.

say: I'd ask for **written hall terms** before selling a family music class.
I'd keep **children's recordings** offline without written permission.
think: **AGI in 2031** may take cues before robot keyboard players arrive around 2034.
**Advert fees** may fall sooner, so a live class must cover its own costs.
do: Offer a **Saturday keyboard group** only with signed room, insurance and ten prepayments covering hire and teaching time.
Keep **sound levels safe** and get written family permission before sharing any child's recording.
Repeat **after 2031** only with ten renewals and safe, written hall terms; refund if only seven pay.
feel: I feel **anxious** because cue income may shrink before a new group pays.
S3.quote: I will not spend our mortgage reserve on a room full of empty chairs.
fieldNote: Her **ten-family gate** covers the hall and her time instead of using emergency savings.
She requires **safe sound levels** and written permission before public use of children's playing.

steps.text: Book hall only with written room and insurance terms
Start group only if ten families prepay hire and teaching time
Keep sound safe and obtain written family consent before sharing recordings
Repeat after 2031 with ten renewals covering hire/teaching, signed room/insurance and safe sound; refund seven

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell local families we have five years to make live music lessons worth paying for. I'd ask the community hall for a proper room fee and safe sound limits before booking anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2031 could take cues and lesson plans, while robot players may follow around 2034. Ordinary software may cheapen my advert cues sooner, so a paid live class would need to earn its way in the warning years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I'll offer a separate Saturday family keyboard group only if the hall signs its room and insurance terms, ten families prepay enough to cover hire and my teaching time, and the sound level is safe for children. By 2031 I'll repeat it only if ten renew; in the first year after AGI, I'll keep it only while those paid places, room terms and safe levels hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about cue fees fading while I test a class. I will not spend our mortgage reserve on a room full of empty chairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the hall available, and what if seven sign up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hall manager has mentioned a Saturday slot, not offered it. If only seven families pay, I'll refund them and wait, because seven fees do not cover the hire and my time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the class protect the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll demonstrate on my own keyboard at a safe volume, and each family can use its own small instrument. I will not put a child's playing online without written family permission.

say: I'd seek a **posted music-director role** with paid hours.
I'd keep **current pupils** until a congregation signs a real offer.
think: At **53 in 2036**, I still need a wage for the mortgage.
**Cue income** may fade earlier, while robot players follow around 2039.
do: Ask two **congregations** about actual director qualifications and paid hours this year.
Aim for **twelve months saved** by 2036 from spare paid pupil and band fees after household bills.
Apply **after 2036** if cues fall, only for posted qualifying director work with pickup and mortgage-covering signed net pay.
feel: I feel **anxious** about earlier cue loss while I look for a genuine paid director role.
S4.quote: Faith is part of my week, yet it cannot substitute for a written salary.
fieldNote: Her **traditional community ties** point to paid congregational work without assuming a vacancy exists.
Her **director move** requires a posted role, accepted degree, child pickup and signed net pay after travel.

steps.text: Ask two congregations for director requirements and paid hours
Aim for twelve months saved by 2036 from spare paid pupil/band fees after household bills
Apply after 2036 if cues fall and posted director job accepts degree
Keep pupils until signed director offer: accepted degree, pickup and net-after-travel pay covering mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the church musicians that ten years is enough to build a paid music-director route, if the congregation and pay are real. I'd want the role advertised with hours, not passed around as a favour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 in 2036, with a mortgage, and robot players may reach venues around 2039. Cues could lose value sooner; a steady director wage would help, but I will not give up good teaching income on a verbal promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll ask two local congregations what qualifications and paid hours their music directors need. By 2036 I'll aim for twelve months of expenses saved from spare paid pupil and band fees after household bills. In the first year after AGI, if cue work falls, I'll apply only for a posted role accepting my bachelor's, with a timetable fitting child pickup and signed net pay after travel covering the mortgage; I'll keep pupils until that offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about cue fees disappearing before 2036, but I have time to seek steadier work. Faith is part of my week, yet it cannot substitute for a written salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a paid music-director vacancy now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One congregation has a volunteer choir leader, not a paid vacancy. I'll ask what a real director job would include before putting it in our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you leave your pupils?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Amir and I will check the actual hours against the children's pickup and the mortgage. I will not cancel eight paid pupils because someone says the committee likes my playing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because cue fees could fall before I secure another paid position. Written band dates, an actual qualified college vacancy and full lender costs if lessons also shrink would help us choose.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what a family class costs before anybody plays a note. Ten paid places must cover both the room and the person teaching in it.

headlineQuote: Ten paid places must cover both the room and the person teaching in it.
portrait: Beth is a **43-year-old keyboardist** with a music bachelor's, partner, two children and a mortgage.
Her **higher pay** and nine-month reserve buffer delays but not ongoing lost cue fees.
She uses **AI daily** for paperwork and checks a new accompaniment tool against her own playing.
She seeks **paid live classes** and real director work while keeping pupils until a written offer.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** could remove cue fees before a replacement paid job exists.
whatWouldHelp: **Written band dates**, a qualifying vacancy and full lender costs would help the household plan.
